title: When a Cat Co-Authored a Paper in a Leading Physics Journal (1975)
description:

body:
in Physics, Random |   	October 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Back in 1975, Jack H. Het­her­ing­ton, a physics pro­fes­sor at Michi­gan State Uni­ver­si­ty, wrote a research paper on low–temperature physics for the respect­ed sci­en­tif­ic jour­nal Phys­i­cal Review Let­ters. Before send­ing it off, Het­her­ing­ton asked a col­league to review the paper, just to make sure it cov­ered the right bases. What hap­pened next Het­her­ing­ton explained in the 1982 book, More Ran­dom Walks in Sci­ence:
Before I sub­mit­ted [the arti­cle], I asked a col­league to read it over and he said, ‘It’s a fine paper, but they’ll send it right back.’ He explained that that is because of the Edi­tor’s rule that the word “we” should not be used in a paper with only a sin­gle author. Chang­ing the paper to the imper­son­al seemed too dif­fi­cult now, and it was all writ­ten and typed; there­fore, after an evening’s thought, I sim­ply asked the sec­re­tary to change the title page to include the name of the fam­i­ly cat, a Siamese called Chester, sired one sum­mer by Willard (one of the few unfixed male Siamese cats in Aspen, Col­orado). I added the ini­tials F D in front of the name to stand for Felix Domes­ti­cus and thus cre­at­ed F D C Willard.
The edi­tors even­tu­al­ly accept­ed the paper, “Two‑, Three‑, and Four-Atom Exchange Effects in bcc 3 He.” And the ruse last­ed until, remem­bers Het­her­ing­ton, “a vis­i­tor [came to the uni­ver­si­ty and] asked to talk to me, and since I was unavail­able asked to talk with Willard. Every­one laughed and soon the cat was out of the bag.” (Pun sure­ly intend­ed.) Appar­ent­ly only the jour­nal edi­tors did­n’t find humor in the joke.

Above, you can see F.D.C. Willard’s sig­na­ture (a paw print) on the front page of the arti­cle. The web­site, Today­I­Found­Out, has much more on this enchant­i­ng lit­tle sto­ry.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: The Dark Story Behind Edgar Allan Poe’s Most Famous Photograph, Taken Four Days After a Laudanum Overdose
description:
in History, Literature, Photography |   	October 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In the Hal­loween sea­son, one Amer­i­can writer comes to mind mo
body:
in History, Literature, Photography |   	October 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In the Hal­loween sea­son, one Amer­i­can writer comes to mind more often than any oth­er: Edgar Allan Poe. That owes in large part to his famous­ly macabre tales like “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” and “The Masque of the Red Death,” writ­ten though they may have been with bare­ly con­cealed con­tempt for their sen­sa­tion-seek­ing mag­a­zine read­er­ship. But it also has to do with the image of the man him­self. Or rather, it has to do with one image in par­tic­u­lar: a daguerreo­type pho­to­graph tak­en on Novem­ber 9, 1848, at a Prov­i­dence stu­dio that has inspired prac­ti­cal­ly every rep­re­sen­ta­tion of Poe in pop­u­lar cul­ture since.
Known as Ulti­ma Thule, this famous por­trait was in fact just one of per­haps ten daguerreo­types for which Poe sat in his life­time. Inven­tor Louis Daguer­re’s ear­ly pho­to­graph­ic process, which used sil­ver-coat­ed cop­per plates, fas­ci­nat­ed Poe, who in an 1840 news­pa­per arti­cle called it “the most impor­tant, and per­haps the most extra­or­di­nary tri­umph of mod­ern sci­ence.” He described its prod­uct as “infi­nite­ly more accu­rate in its rep­re­sen­ta­tion than any paint­ing by human hands,” though any­one sit­ting for a pic­ture did have to sit still for min­utes on end, result­ing in not just the unsmil­ing vis­ages we asso­ciate with nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry pho­tog­ra­phy, but also in a com­bi­na­tion of dis­com­fort and slight blur­ring that can look vague­ly oth­er­world­ly.
That qual­i­ty may actu­al­ly have enhanced the aura of Ulti­ma Thule, which painter Michael J. Deas calls “the image of the trag­ic roman­tic poet: solemn, detached, con­sumed by his own wild­ly self-destruc­tive nature.” It sure­ly also made a dif­fer­ence that the por­trait was made, in the words of poet Her­vey Allen, “prob­a­bly at the very hour when he looked the worst that he had ever looked in his life.” He’d been tak­en to the stu­dio by a stranger with whom he’d spent the pre­vi­ous night binge-drink­ing. Just four days before that, he’d unsuc­cess­ful­ly attempt­ed sui­cide by lau­danum over­dose, a rash action tak­en after the rejec­tion of his mar­riage pro­pos­al by Sarah Helen Whit­man, a wid­owed poet he had­n’t known long — and who would give her suit­or’s immor­tal por­trait its Latin name, bor­rowed from his poem “Dream-Land.”
The orig­i­nal daguerreo­type, for which the stu­dio prob­a­bly paid the by-then notable, still per­pet­u­al­ly hard-up Poe to sit, remained with its mak­ers until it van­ished around 1860, and its where­abouts have remained unknown ever since. But copies have allowed gen­er­a­tion after gen­er­a­tion of read­ers to behold Poe’s trou­bled vis­age when what Whit­man called “all the stormy grandeur of that via Dolorosa had left its sullen shad­ow on his brow.” Through the drunk­en chaos and pover­ty of his life, the writer him­self could see things to come. “The con­se­quences of any new sci­en­tif­ic inven­tion will, at the present day exceed, by very much, the wildest expec­ta­tions of the most imag­i­na­tive,” he wrote, an obser­va­tion true enough of pho­tog­ra­phy 178 years ago, and no doubt even truer of what we use to make images today.

He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: In 'Aeolus,' DRIFT Suspends Illuminated Glass Rods in a Sculpture of the Wind
description: Combining the elemental rhythms with human-made materials, DRIFT’s latest sculptural choreography invites visitors to consider their connection to
body:
Combining the elemental rhythms with human-made materials, DRIFT’s latest sculptural choreography invites visitors to consider their connection to nature in an interactive experience influenced by the planet’s intrinsic processes and systems. “Aeolus” is named for the ancient Greek deity of the wind and comprises an environment characterized by numerous glass rods with tiny lights inside. These are activated by visitors’ movements.
“Like wind itself, the work only fully exists through interaction,” say Lonneke Gordijn and Ralph Nauta, founders of the Amsterdam-based design studio in a statement. “It is both still and in motion, fixed yet constantly changing.” Light and glass were chosen to further represent ephemerality and transitions. Glass can be so light and clear it appears spectral, and light is immaterial like the wind: it may be here one moment and gone the next.

“Aeolus” remains on view through October 25 at Carpenters inside of Ladbroke Hall in London. The studio has also announced the forthcoming DRIFT Museum, an 8,000-square-meter space inside of the Van Gendt Hallen in Amsterdam slated to open in early 2027. Follow updates on DRIFT’s Instagram.

title: Come Face-to-Face with the Lion Nebula in the James Webb Space Telescope's Portrait
description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has captured some remarkable phenomena in space, from the Horsehead Nebula to the unbelievable “Pillars of Creat
body:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has captured some remarkable phenomena in space, from the Horsehead Nebula to the unbelievable “Pillars of Creation.” Things just got a little bit wilder with brilliant images of the Lion Nebula (NGC 2392) captured by the telescope’s NIRCam (Near Infrared Camera) and MIRI (Mid Infrared Instrument). The shape is formed by the remains of a dying star now at a phase known as a white dwarf, when a very dense stellar core remains as it sheds its outer layers. On NGC 2392, the bright center looks like a little nose.
“The central dying star is so hot that its radiation is ‘cooking’ everything from the inside and producing a bubble of ionized hydrogen gas as it does,” NASA says. “The gas bubble, which is the lion’s ‘face,’ features cavernous shells and rings with tendrils that are expanding and destroying dust upon encounter.” The lion’s “mane” is actually the inside of one of these shells, illuminated by the star’s core.
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope’s mid-infrared image of planetary nebula NGC 2392, nicknamed the Lion Nebula, highlights the varying dust structures. Some dust is being destroyed by the dying central star’s radiation, while some dust filaments manage to survive.
From the human perspective of time, nebulae such as this one don’t seem to change very quickly. “It’s taken several thousand years for the gas and dust to be shaped in this way, and it continues to change as the star drives away the material,” NASA says. The Lion Nebula is changing rather quickly in astronomical terms, however, and astronomers estimate that it will fully disperse in about 10,000 years. (via Kottke)

title: Paris Students Block Louvre Entrance, Forcing Closure
description:
News
                Students from the independent École du Louvre and the National School of Fine Arts are leading the ongoing
body:
News
                Students from the independent École du Louvre and the National School of Fine Arts are leading the ongoing action. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Students block the entrance to the Louvre Museum in protest of the lack of resources and access to culture. (photo Basile Dubouis / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            Dozens of students from the École du Louvre, a higher education arts institution in the Louvre Palace in Paris, began blocking the main entrance of the Louvre Museum today, October 19, as nationwide protests over the overcrowded and underresourced conditions of France's education system reach the one-month mark. The blockade prevented the institution from opening at 9 am as students from the grande école, which is located on the museum grounds but operates independently, played music, held up protest art, and distributed leaflets to passersby that read, "We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world's largest museum." Members of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour trade union also stated that students from the National School of Fine Arts are taking part in the demonstration, according to European outlets. The museum did not open today, and it remains unclear whether it will tomorrow. The Louvre has not replied to Hyperallergic's immediate request for comment. A flyer informing visitors about the blockade (photo Dimitar Dilkoff / AFP via Getty Images)What began as a protest at one underdeveloped suburban high school outside Paris over crumbling infrastructure, grueling hours, staffing cuts, and a litany of other issues within the French education system last month has surged into nationwide strikes over the diminished ability to study and work in France. Separate from the peaceful demonstrations, some individuals began stealing from shops and setting storefronts aflame across Paris and other French cities over the weekend, resulting in violent clashes with the police. Riot police reportedly threw tear gas and launched water cannons at some protesters, and beat others with batons, according to the BBC. Though the French government has not released figures about the total number of protester injuries, according to the French Interior Ministry, nearly 2,400 people were arrested, and about 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured. Students and protesters hold up flyers and play music in front of the Louvre (photo Quentin de Groeve / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)"French students and workers are currently fighting their government and its anti-public-services politics," one of the leaflets distributed at the protest reads. "We thank you for your interest in French culture, and for standing with our fight to study, to work, and to live freely in good conditions."

title: Rosana Paulino Reads the Archive Against Those Who Made It
description:
Interview
                “This history is dirty,” says the Brazilian artist, who sees the colonial past as an active force in h
body:
Interview
                “This history is dirty,” says the Brazilian artist, who sees the colonial past as an active force in her country’s present.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Rosana Paulino at her exhibition ¿História Natural? at the Vera List Center for Art and Politics in New York City (photo Daniela Mayer/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            On Monday, October 5, the day after a contentious first round sent Brazil’s presidential election to a runoff, Rosana Paulino sat in the New School’s Arnold and Sheila Aronson Galleries beside a wall hung with her natural-pigment drawings of small figures curled within seeds. Most, she was quick to point out, are studies; only two counted as works. She tears up the drawings that don’t meet her standards — or did, until her studio assistants began hiding the discards for her archive. Paulino is an admitted perfectionist; in her hands, precision is a form of respect.The first Afro-Brazilian woman to earn a PhD in visual arts in Brazil, Paulino sees the colonial past as an active force in her country’s present, visible above all in the violence, archival and literal, against Black people, especially women. Her solo exhibition ¿História Natural?, organized by the Vera List Center for Art and Politics, is on view through November 1. It centers on its namesake, the 2016 artist’s book that won Paulino the 2025–27 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice, along with its $25,000 award. The book’s pages pair linocut and drypoint with altered prints of photographs made for the Harvard naturalist Louis Agassiz’s 1865–66 expedition to Brazil, collaged and stitched onto paper and fabric. Nothing is incidental; even the lettering is smeared with intention. “This history is dirty,” she said while leafing through its pages.This year, Brazil’s pavilion at the Venice Biennale, curated by Diane Lima, took its title from Paulino’s 2024 drawings of the same name: Comigo ninguém pode (“No one can beat me”). The phrase suits her: On her nation’s history, she gives little ground. A teacher for many years, Paulino patiently explains rather than defends her positions. She reads the archive against the people who made it. In our conversation below, she asks you to do the same.This interview has been translated from Portuguese by the author and edited for length and clarity.Rosana Paulino's 2016 book ¿História Natural? (photo Daniela Mayer/Hyperallergic)Hyperallergic: For ¿História Natural?, you’re working with, and against, the colonizer’s own format: the illustrated naturalist album. European expeditions came to Brazil to picture it, and the images went back to Europe, where they shaped how the country was imagined. What drew you to the form?Rosana Paulino: The book really is a kind of treatise on how Black people, and Brazil itself, have been represented. As you said, when Brazil was invaded, Europeans came to map the country. First the traveling painters, and later photography. That album format was very common: The country was mapped and the results sent back to Europe. I drew on that format because it produced the first images of Brazil. It’s the reference for this album. And why do it? I think that’s the real question. Because Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself. Brazil often used those same images, made by Europeans, to represent itself, without looking at them critically. When I was a student, around age 12, those images were everywhere in schoolbooks. They weren’t images Brazilians made to understand what Brazil is. They were images made by foreigners for foreigners, which Brazil brought home without any critique. Until quite recently, when schoolbooks discussed slavery, those were the images of Black people you saw. So the book really grows out of those images.
                  
                      
                        Interview
                      
                      
                        Rosana Paulino

title: Diasporican Abstraction: A Cross-Border Cartography of Puerto Rican Abstraction
description:
Announcement
                More than sixty artists explore migration, memory, and identity in this survey of Puerto Rican abstracti
body:
Announcement
                More than sixty artists explore migration, memory, and identity in this survey of Puerto Rican abstraction across and beyond the archipelago. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Left: Raphael Collazo, “Arcana Mundi (Mysteries of the World)", 1985; Top right: Olga Albizu, “Blue Oil”, 1974; Bottom right: Raphael Montañez Ortíz, “Archaeological Find #22: The Aftermath”, 1961
    
        
            What happens when our understanding of Puerto Ricanness is no longer organized around territory? Diasporican Abstraction: Identities Beyond Representation, the new exhibition at the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico (MACPR), invites us to do just that: consider diasporic experiences that converge and intertwine with Puerto Rico beyond its territory. Curated by Abdiel D. Segarra Ríos, the exhibition is the conclusion of a decade of research that brings together more than sixty artists from different generations and geographic backgrounds. Their trajectories extend from Puerto Rico to the United States, Canada, Europe, and Australia, intersecting with those of artists from the Caribbean, Central America, and South America. The curatorial approach establishes dialogues between works spanning generations that share concerns with color, form, materials as well as territory, ancestrality, corporeality, and the natural and built environment. Rather than constructing a chronology of Puerto Rican abstraction in the diaspora, the exhibition proposes a web of relationships, conceived as ecosystems that unfold across the four galleries it occupies. The exhibition moves beyond the structures and categories through which art history is written and questions the need for strictly Puerto Rican, Caribbean or American narratives about abstraction. It recognizes that experiences of movement and belonging generate their own visual languages, independent of physical presence or allegiance to a country's shared imaginary or visual repertoire. Perhaps most importantly, the exhibition seeks to bring visibility to artists and aesthetics marginalized in the construction of Puerto Rican art narratives. It fosters a dialogue between works from the collection of El Museo del Barrio in New York, many presented for the first time in Puerto Rico, and pieces from MAC's Permanent Collection, as well as new commissions. This encounter evokes the promise of return embedded in the diasporic experience while suggesting that Puerto Rico is not singular and has no immutable center, but rather depends on who is looking and from where.The exhibition features works by Olga Albizu, Candida Álvarez, Rafael Ferrer, Ivelisse Jiménez, Zilia Sánchez, Edra Soto, Gisela Colón, Nayda Collazo-Llorens, Tony Bechara, Awilda Sterling Duprey, Lee Quiñones, and Ángel Otero, alongside those of fifty other artists from different generations and backgrounds. Rather than simply redrawing the geographic map of Puerto Rican artistic production, these artists question the cross-border realities of Puerto Ricanness, using abstraction as a tool to dislocate identity from territory and reconstruct it through multiple forms of belonging.Diasporican Abstraction: Identities Beyond Representation will be on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art of Puerto Rico from September 26, 2026, through May 2027.
